intro: KUB 14.8 is the main manuscript of Muršili II's 'Second Plague Prayer', addressed to the Storm-god of Ḫatti. Muršili reports that two old tablets and oracle inquiries revealed the causes of the plague: the neglected offering to the river Mala, and the breach of the oath sworn with Egypt in the Kuruštamma affair, which led to his father's Egyptian campaign and to a plague brought home by Egyptian prisoners. He confesses his father's sin, offers restitution, and asks to be told in a dream or by oracle if some other cause lies behind the dying.

paras.en: […] … […] let it be [ascertain]ed (by oracle); or […] it […], or let a [man of god] declare (it). But the gods […] me […]. […] in the land of Ḫatti the plague did not get better; [it op]pressed (the land?).

[…] of my gods, the bread-offerers [and libation-pourers(?)] who were [le]ft, they [kept dy]ing. [The matter(?)] became still more grievous, and of the gods […] […] I [fo]und two old tablets. One tablet [concerned the offering to the river Mala]: long ago the former kings used to present the offering to the river Mala; but all the while that there has been [dying] in the land of Ḫatti since the days of my father, we have never performed the offering to the river Mala.

[The second tabl]et concerned the town of Kuruštamma: how the [Storm-god] of Ḫatti carried the men of Kuruštamma off to the land of Egypt, and how the Storm-god of Ḫatti made a [trea]ty for them with the men of Ḫatti, so that they were put under oath by the Storm-god of Ḫatti. Although the men of Ḫatti and the men of Egypt were bound by oath by the Storm-god of Ḫatti, the men of Ḫatti went and turned about(?), and the men of Ḫatti quickly broke the oath of the god. My father sent troops and chariotry, and they attacked the border of Egypt, the land of Amka; and again he sent (them), and again they attacked. When the men of Egypt became afraid, they came and even asked my father for a son of his for the kingship. But when my father gave them his son and they led him away, they killed him. My father became enraged(?) (kappilazzatta, a Luwian word), went into the land of Egypt, attacked the land of Egypt, and struck down the troops and chariotry of Egypt.

And then too the Storm-god of Ḫatti, my lord, upheld my father by his verdict, so that he overcame the troops and chariotry of the land of Egypt and struck them down. But when the [captive] people whom they had seized were brought back to the land of Ḫatti, a plague broke out among the prisoners, and they began to die. When they had carried the prisoners into the land of Ḫatti, the prisoners brought the plague into the land of Ḫatti, and from that day on there has been continual dying in the land of Ḫatti. When I found that tablet about the land of Egypt, I made it the subject of an oracle inquiry to the god: 'Has this matter been brought about by the Storm-god of Ḫatti, because the men of Egypt and the men of Ḫatti had been put under oath by the Storm-god of Ḫatti,

and because the Damnaššara-deities (are) in the temple of the Storm-god of Ḫatti, my lord, while it was the men of Ḫatti who quickly broke the word? Has it perhaps become a cause of anger for the Storm-god of Ḫatti, my lord?' And it was confirmed (by the oracle). On account of the plague I also made the offering to the river Mala the subject of an oracle inquiry, and there too it was confirmed that I must step before the Storm-god of Ḫatti, my lord. See, I have confessed […] the [s]in: it is so, we did it. […] before me(?) […] … in the time of my father … […] I know full well(?) […] … the matter; and the Storm-god […] angry on account of (it) […] there is continual dying.

And the offering […] [I] offered […] … you […]. But […] of the river Mala […] me. See, as for what (concerns) [the river M]ala, […] my lords, […] you let the offering [of the river Ma]la go(?) (EGIR-an tarna-, 'leave behind'?) […]; let me see to it(?), and I will perform it(?). In which […] gods, my lords, have pity […], and within […] let the plague be put right!

Storm-god of Ḫat[ti] […] my lords: so it comes about that people keep sinning. My father too [sin]ned and transgressed the [wo]rd of the Storm-god of Ḫatti, my lord, but I have not sinned in any way. Yet so it comes about that the sin of the father reaches his son; and so the sin of my father has reached me too. See, I have now confessed it before the Storm-god of Ḫatti, my lord, and the gods, my lords: it is so, we did it. And because I have confessed the sin of my father, let the soul of the Storm-god of Ḫatti, my lord, and of the gods, my lords, be soothed again. Have pity on me again, and once more send the plague away from the land of Ḫatti. And these few bread-offerers and libation-pourers who remain — […] they [d]ie on me (§8 asks that they die no more).

See, I am making a plea to the Storm-god, my lord, on account of the plague. Hear me, Storm-god of Ḫatti, my lord, and keep me alive! And I (say) this to you: a bird takes refuge in its taptappa- (nest or cage), and the taptappa- keeps it alive. Or if something weighs upon some servant, he makes a plea to his lord; his lord hears him and [has pity] on him, and whatever weighs upon him, he puts it right for him. Or if some servant has a sin but confesses the sin before his lord, his lord may do to him then whatever he (will); but because he has confessed his sin before his lord, his lord's soul is soothed, and the lord will not call that servant to account again. I have confessed the sin of my father: it is so, we did it. If some compensation (is due): from that plague a great deal (has been paid) already […] … the prisoners of war whom they brought from the land of Egypt, and the deportees whom […]; and what Ḫattuša has paid back through the plague — [has] it [not] already become twentyfold? Yet the soul of the Storm-god of Ḫatti, my lord, [and] of the gods, my lords, is not soothed at all. Or if you intend to impose some separate compensation on me, tell it to me in a dream, and I will give it to you.

See, I too am praying to the Storm-god of Ḫatti, my lord: keep me alive! And if people are perhaps dying because of this matter, then while I am setting it right again, let those bread-offerers and libation-pourers of the gods who remain die no more.

But if people are dying for some other reason, then let me either see it in a dream, or let it be [ascert]ained by oracle, or let a man of god declare it. Or […] to [the priests(?)] … I have given orders to [a]ll, and they will regularly sleep in purity (to receive dreams?) […]. […] [of Ḫatti], my lord, keep me alive! And the gods, my lords, […] let them reveal (it)! And there it […] […] … for (which) reason people are dying […] […] … bronze needle(?), [with(?)] a šarpa- (?) […].
